title: The fair-discrepancy propagation conjecture for fully balanced matrices
statement:
Let $A\in\mathbb{M}_{n\times m}(\mathbb{R})$ be a fully balanced matrix. For each row $i$, let

$$
M_i=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{ij}
$$

be its average discrepancy. If, for a fixed $1\leq i\leq n$, one has

$$
|M_i-a_{ij}|<\epsilon
$$

for the relevant entries $j$, then $|M_i-a_{ij}|<\epsilon$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$.

**Fair-discrepancy propagation conjecture.** If one fixed row has discrepancy less than $\epsilon$, then every row has discrepancy less than $\epsilon$.

The claim concerns propagation of a fair discrepancy from one row to all rows of a fully balanced matrix. The supplied text gives no resolution or additional context.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.07542

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of October 2018).
source_name: Theophilus Agama and Gael Kibiti, “Balanced matrices”, arXiv:1810.07542 (2026).

progress.label: Open · progress reported
progress.tldr: A reader-submitted example appears to disprove the conjecture, but it has not been independently checked, so the general question remains open.
progress.summary:
The statement is recorded as Conjecture 6.6 in *Balanced matrices*: fair discrepancy in one row of a fully balanced matrix should propagate to every row. No published proof or disproof was found.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.07542v3)*

**Known results**

- For positive fully balanced matrices of size $2\times2$, fair discrepancy along rows is equivalent to fair discrepancy along columns (Theorem 6.4).
- In the same $2\times2$ setting, fair discrepancy in one row implies fair discrepancy in all rows (Proposition 6.5).


**Community submission (unverified)**

The August 22, 2026 submission argues that $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&5&5\\1&5&7\\7&5&1\end{pmatrix}$ has equal row and column squared energies, while its first row has zero discrepancy and its second row violates the condition for $\varepsilon=1$; scaling is claimed to extend this to every $\varepsilon>0$.


Current status (as of September 2026): The positive $2\times2$ case is settled, while the general conjecture remains open and the submitted counterexample is unverified.

*Caveats. The proposed counterexample has no independent source or mathematical verification.*

solutions.body:
**Counterexample to discrepancy propagation, even for strictly positive, exactly balanced matrices.**

For a matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, write

$$
R_i=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{ij}^{2},\qquad
C_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{ij}^{2},\qquad
M_i=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{ij}.
$$

The conjecture asserts that, for a fully balanced matrix and a fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the inequalities

$$
\lvert M_r-a_{rj}\rvert<\varepsilon
\qquad (1\le j\le m)
$$

for one row $r$ imply the corresponding inequalities in every row. Consider the strictly positive integer matrix

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&5&5\\
1&5&7\\
7&5&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its row energies are

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_1&=5^2+5^2+5^2=75,\\
R_2&=1^2+5^2+7^2=75,\\
R_3&=7^2+5^2+1^2=75,
\end{aligned}
$$

and its column energies are

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=5^2+1^2+7^2=75,\\
C_2&=5^2+5^2+5^2=75,\\
C_3&=5^2+7^2+1^2=75.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $A$ is simultaneously horizontally and vertically balanced with exact equality, which is stronger than the approximate balance required in the original definition. Set $\varepsilon=1$. The first row has mean

$$
M_1=\frac{5+5+5}{3}=5,
$$

and therefore

$$
\lvert M_1-a_{1j}\rvert=0<1
\qquad (j=1,2,3).
$$

However, the second row has mean

$$
M_2=\frac{1+5+7}{3}=\frac{13}{3},
$$

so its first entry satisfies

$$
\lvert M_2-a_{21}\rvert
=\left\lvert\frac{13}{3}-1\right\rvert
=\frac{10}{3}>1.
$$

Thus the first row has fair discrepancy while the second does not, disproving the conjecture.

In fact, the obstruction persists for every prescribed tolerance: for any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $t>3\varepsilon/10$ and replace $A$ by $tA$. Every row and column then has squared energy $75t^2$; the first-row deviations remain zero, whereas

$$
\left\lvert M_2(tA)-(tA)_{21}\right\rvert
=\frac{10t}{3}>\varepsilon.
$$

If desired, taking $t\ge1$ also preserves the stronger entrywise condition $(tA)_{ij}\ge1$. Hence neither exact energy balance nor strict positivity restores discrepancy propagation.

*Source:* T. Agama and G. Kibiti, *Balanced matrices*, arXiv:1810.07542v3, Definition 3.1, Conjecture 6.6, and Remark 6.7.
